concept.name: Channel breakout strategy
concept.definition: A trend-entry rule that buys when price exceeds the highest high (or sells when it breaks the lowest low) of a trailing N-period channel, on the premise that a break of an established range marks the start of a sustained move. It is the 'trading range break' rule tested by Brock, Lakonishok and LeBaron (1992) and generalized in Donchian-style systems.
concept.intuition: A market coiled in a box stores energy; a break beyond the box means buyers or sellers finally overwhelmed the range boundary, and the absence of nearby reference points lets the move run.
concept.mechanics: Compute the channel as the rolling N-day high and low; enter long one tick above the N-day high or short one tick below the N-day low, with stops inside the prior range or ATR-based. Brock-Lakonishok-LeBaron tested trading-range-break rules on the Dow from 1897 to 1986, finding buy and sell signals asymmetric in return and volatility relative to random-walk, AR(1), GARCH-M, and EGARCH nulls.
concept.formula: Long signal: P_t > max(H over t-N..t-1); short signal: P_t < min(L over t-N..t-1).
concept.failure_modes: Sideways, mean-reverting markets generate repeated false breakouts whose accumulated small losses define the strategy's cost; the rule is structurally many small losers against few big winners, so choppy regimes bleed it.
concept.misconceptions: That the channel length is the secret; results are far more sensitive to regime, costs, and exit rules than to the exact lookback, and the academic evidence is descriptive of historical data rather than a proven predictive law.
concept.example: With a 50-day high at $102, a stop-entry buy triggers at $102.05; the protective stop sits at the 10-day low of $96, risking about 6% of price on the position.

citations.source: Brock, Lakonishok & LeBaron, 'Simple Technical Trading Rules and the Stochastic Properties of Stock Returns', Journal of Finance 47(5), 1992, 1731-1764 (EconPapers record)
